lines.text: This is Sketch2Sim, built today at MLH Hacktoberfest Hack Day Batam.

Every hardware idea starts as a sketch on paper. Turning that sketch into a working circuit is the slow part: picking pins, adding resistors, writing firmware, and then hunting for the one wire you put in backwards.
So we asked a simple question. What if the sketch was the source code?
Draw your circuit right in the browser, or just snap a photo of your notebook, and hit compile.
Gemma 4 reads the drawing. The boxes, the lines, even the handwritten notes. And it returns a complete circuit: the parts, the wiring with a reason for every pin, and the Arduino firmware.

But we don't trust the model blindly. Every answer goes through a deterministic validator. It locks each part to a real Wokwi component, fixes pin names, adds missing resistors, and flips parts that are wired backwards. And it shows you every repair it made.
Now paste both files into Wokwi, a real circuit simulator, and press play. The traffic light from a pencil sketch is running.

Five hand-drawn sketches. Five circuits running in Wokwi. We cut compile time from about a hundred seconds to thirty. And if the network drops on stage, presets fall back to a saved run, clearly labeled as cached.
Next up: ESP32 and Arduino UNO Q, more parts, and a classroom mode for vocational schools, where students lose hours to one wrong jumper wire.
Sketch2Sim. Open source, MIT licensed, built with Gemma 4 and Claude Code. Try it today.
